title: Population ageing is increasingly a women’s issue: longer lives coexist with poorer late-life health, care burdens, and economic insecurity
source_unit: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Gender matters in an ageing world: The case for gender-responsive policies
geography: Global population ageing, with comparisons across income groups and policy implications for older women, health, social protection, care, and economic participation

denominator.unit: global population aged 60 years or older

older_population_2050.unit: projected people aged 60 or older in 2050

demographic_mechanism.value: population ageing is accelerating in nearly all regions through sustained fertility decline and improved survival at older ages

observations.method: UN DESA policy brief using World Population Prospects 2024 and additional demographic and policy datasets.
observations.uncertainty: Population projections depend on fertility, mortality, migration, and projection assumptions; aggregate age counts do not describe health, income, living arrangements, or care needs.
observations.subgroup: Older persons, families, care systems, governments, and regions at different stages of demographic transition.
observations.counterinterpretation: Ageing reflects longer survival and can support longer productive and civic lives when health, income, care, and participation systems adapt.

observations.period: 2000-2050; older women as a share of the older population

older_women_2050.unit: projected women aged 60 or older in 2050

share_2050.unit: percent of the global population aged 60 or older projected to be women in 2050

low_middle_income_growth.value: the number of women aged 60 or older in low- and middle-income countries is projected to more than double by 2050

observations.method: UN DESA age-sex population estimates and projections with income-group comparison.
observations.uncertainty: Projection categories and income-group comparisons do not show the distribution of wealth, disability, care, or legal rights among older women.
observations.subgroup: Older women, especially those living in low- and middle-income countries, and the families and institutions that support them.
observations.counterinterpretation: A growing population of older women is also a source of knowledge, care, paid work, civic participation, and social contribution when barriers are removed.

denominator.unit: global population aged 80 years or older

women_80_2050.unit: projected women aged 80 or older in 2050

women_share_80_2025.unit: percent of the population aged 80 or older who were women in 2025

women_share_80_2050.unit: projected percent of the population aged 80 or older who will be women in 2050

observations.method: UN DESA age-sex population estimates and projections for the oldest age groups.
observations.uncertainty: Counts do not measure healthy ageing, disability-free years, living arrangements, or formal and informal care demand.
observations.subgroup: Women at advanced ages, caregivers, health and social-care systems, households, and communities adapting to longevity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Longer survival can create substantial social and economic value when age-friendly environments, care, health, and income systems support autonomy.

observations.period: 2000-2050; later-life health and economic security for women

denominator.unit: global older-women health, income, and policy synthesis frame

female_life_expectancy_at_60_2000.unit: years of remaining life expectancy at age 60 for women in 2000

female_life_expectancy_at_60_2025.unit: years of remaining life expectancy at age 60 for women in 2025

female_life_expectancy_at_60_2050.unit: projected years of remaining life expectancy at age 60 for women in 2050

health_inequality.value: women tend to spend a higher proportion of later life in poor health or with disability despite living longer on average

economic_security.value: lower lifetime earnings, interrupted careers, and limited pension coverage can leave older women more financially vulnerable while they continue to provide care and support

observations.method: UN DESA synthesis of demographic trends and policy implications for health, social protection, care, economic resources, and participation.
observations.uncertainty: The brief identifies broad mechanisms and policy priorities; it does not estimate individual causal effects or separate every contribution of health, work, pension, family, and care systems.
observations.subgroup: Older women, women with interrupted careers, unpaid caregivers, women with disabilities, pension systems, health systems, and families.
observations.counterinterpretation: Gender-responsive health, pension, care, legal, and participation policies can convert longer lives into greater autonomy and contribution rather than vulnerability.

related_sources.claim: UN DESA population-ageing page provides complementary older-person data and policy context.
UN World Population Prospects provides the demographic estimates and projections underlying the brief.

boundary: This record adds a gendered-ageing route across population growth, longevity, later-life health, pension and income insecurity, unpaid care, and policy visibility. It uses UN DESA aggregate demographic estimates and policy synthesis, not respondent-level ageing histories, individual health records, household care diaries, causal pension effects, or proof that ageing produces the same outcome for all women.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UN DESA policy brief page and accessible brief text reviewed for older-population counts, older-women and oldest-old projections, life expectancy at age 60, health, economic-security, care, and gender-responsive policy findings.
